lessons.title: The catchment as a system
lessons.html:
What is a catchment?

A catchment (or watershed) is the area of land from which all rainfall drains to a common point: a stream, river, dam or wetland. Everything that happens on the land in a catchment affects the water downstream. Ploughing a steep slope, overgrazing, invasive trees, informal settlements without sanitation, mines and feedlots all change the quantity and quality of water reaching the next user.

Why integrated management?

Traditionally, land, water, forests and settlements were managed by different authorities and owners with little coordination. Integrated catchment management (ICM) treats the catchment as one system and brings land and water users together to manage it for social, economic and environmental benefits. In South Africa, the National Water Act 36 of 1998 is built on this idea: water is managed by water management areas, with catchment management agencies and water user associations, and a Reserve of water must be kept for basic human needs and for ecosystems before other uses are allocated.

Parts of a catchment

  • Upper catchment – mountain grasslands, fynbos and wetlands that act like sponges; source areas often critical for water supply.
  • Middle catchment – farming, forestry, settlements.
  • Lower catchment – larger rivers, floodplains, towns and estuaries.
  • Riparian zones – vegetation along rivers that filters runoff and stabilises banks.
  • Wetlands – store water, reduce floods, purify water and support biodiversity.

Key catchment issues

  • Invasive alien trees (wattle, pine, gum) using large volumes of water in the upper catchment and riparian zones.
  • Erosion and siltation of dams.
  • Pollution from fertiliser, pesticides, manure, sewage and industry.
  • Over-abstraction and unlawful water use.
  • Wetland drainage and cultivation in riparian zones.

lessons.title: Putting ICM into practice
lessons.html:
Steps in implementing ICM

  1. Establish a forum. Bring together farmers, communities, traditional authorities, municipalities, industry, conservation agencies, the water department and catchment agency. Agree on purpose and terms of reference.
  2. Build a shared picture. Map land use, water sources, users, problem areas and sensitive areas (wetlands, springs, riparian zones) using existing data, satellite images and community mapping.
  3. Assess condition. Water quantity and quality monitoring (e.g. flow, turbidity, nutrients, E. coli), biomonitoring of river invertebrates, erosion and invasive plant density.
  4. Agree priorities. Focus on actions with the greatest benefit, often in source areas and hotspots.
  5. Develop an action plan with responsibilities, budget and timelines.
  6. Implement on-the-ground projects.
  7. Monitor, review and adapt.

Typical actions

IssueActions
Invasive plantsClearing with follow-up, prioritising riparian zones and upper catchment
ErosionGrazing management, gully rehabilitation, road drainage
Riparian zonesBuffer strips, fencing, indigenous replanting, no cultivation on the banks
WetlandsBlocking drainage channels, controlling grazing and burning, rehabilitation
PollutionNutrient management plans, safe pesticide handling, manure storage, sanitation
Water useRegistration and licensing of water use, efficient irrigation, metering

Making it work

  • Link actions to benefits that people value: reliable water, better grazing, jobs.
  • Coordinate funding from different programmes.
  • Communicate results with simple indicators and maps.
  • Respect legal processes: water use authorisations and environmental authorisations where required.

Key points

  • A catchment is all land draining to a common point; land use affects water downstream.
  • ICM manages land and water together with all stakeholders.
  • The National Water Act 36 of 1998 requires a Reserve for basic human needs and ecosystems.
  • Protect source areas, wetlands and riparian zones and clear invasive trees.
  • Implement through a forum, shared assessment, priorities, action plan and monitoring.
